variants.note: Steep, often broken into multiple intersecting hips over an irregular plan.
The inherited value from germanic-vernacular (a taxed-narrow-lot urban gable-front logic) does not apply to an American Gilded Age estate house and is corrected here.
Dutch Colonial and Colonial Revival; unrelated to a French Renaissance roof vocabulary.
The opposite move from Beaux-Arts; see balustrade.

roof_form.rule: A steep hipped roof, or a set of intersecting steep hips, is the dominant compositional mass — the style's own proportional_system states there is 'no governing module; proportion is set by the roof, which is designed as an inhabited mass roughly equal in height to the top two storeys.'

tower_pitch.value: steeper than the adjacent principal mass, often conical

roof_pitch.rule: Not less than 14:12, the style's own hard constraint, and typically 14:12 to 20:12 on principal masses. Corrects an inherited 45-degree (=12:12) floor drawn from british-picturesque, which is a full pitch class shallower than what this style's own c02 requires.

variants.note: THE diagnostic move: the style's own diagnostic_tells state 'if the dormers stop at the eave rather than cutting through it, it is not Chateauesque.' Stone surrounds continuous from sill to a pedimented, finialed, or crocketed dormer head.
A twentieth-century attic-conversion device with no place cutting through a chateau's stone-surrounded wall dormers.
Shingle Style and Richardsonian; the low unbroken curve is the opposite move from a wall dormer's vertical stone surround.

dormer.rule: At least two wall dormers must break the cornice line and rise not less than half a storey above it, with stone surrounds continuous from the sill below the cornice to the dormer pediment above. A roof-set dormer beginning entirely above the eave is forbidden as the primary type.

chimney.note: The inherited 'tall-multiple-vertical-accent' canonical variant from british-picturesque already agrees with this style in kind; this delta only adds the style's own hard-constraint numbers (c04), which the ancestor's Gothic/Queen Anne/Baronial framing did not carry.
chimney.rule_append: A minimum 4'-0" x 2'-6" plan footprint, rising not less than 4'-0" above the adjacent ridge, with a corbelled or panelled shaft.

variants.note: Dressed limestone or granite, coursed, with joints under 3/8 in per the style's own diagnostic_tells.
The inherited canonical value, from english-georgian by way of the georgian-colonial-american chain, is a different masonry tradition entirely and is corrected here.
A light-frame cladding; incompatible with load-bearing ashlar construction (c01).
A veneer economy the style's own c05 names directly as one of the reductions that 'destroys it' and produces Queen Anne with a turret instead.

primary_cladding.rule: Load-bearing dressed ashlar, carved on site, not cast or veneered — chateauesque.c01. 'If it is wood, it is not Beaux-Arts' applies here even more strongly: if it is not real coursed stone, it is not Chateauesque.

expression.value: a continuous ashlar plinth or watertable in the same stone as the wall above; no exposed timber sill

foundation_expression.rule: A masonry plinth in the wall's own stone. The inherited value (a timber-frame Sockel clear of grade, from germanic-vernacular) presupposes a light frame this style does not have and is corrected here.

variants.note: Where the corner is turned by a round tower rather than a square quoin.

The inherited value ('no masonry quoin — the corner is a structural timber post') is germanic-vernacular's exposed-timber-frame logic and has no application to a load-bearing ashlar wall; corrected here.

corner_quoin.rule: A real ashlar quoin or a coursed masonry corner, never an exposed frame member.

reveal_depth.note: Raises the inherited 12-24 in floor to the style's own hard minimum of 16 in — the inherited range's bottom third (12-16 in) does not satisfy c01.

jamb_material.value: returned in the same stone as the face

reveal_masonry.note: The inherited 12-24 in band (from mediterranean-vernacular) already overlaps correctly at its upper end; this delta only tightens the floor to match the style's own hard constraint.
reveal_masonry.rule_append: The reveal is not less than 16 in, and jambs are returned in the same stone as the face — chateauesque.c01. Thin-set veneer with a 1 in reveal voids the style outright.

variants.note: Multi-light, per the style's own defining_characteristics: 'multi-light casement or transomed sash.'
The inherited canonical value is drawn from a Victorian/Queen Anne/Baronial finding (british-picturesque) unrelated to this style's own stated glazing.

window_type.rule: Multi-light casement, or a fixed sash with a transom, behind a round- or basket-arched stone surround — never a plain double-hung sash.

variants.note: The inherited Georgian date-ladder (12/12 through 6/6) belongs to georgian-colonial-american and has no application here.
Part of the inherited Georgian date-ladder (georgian-colonial-american); the wide flat muntin grid reads as Colonial, not as a leaded chateau casement.
Same Georgian date-ladder; forbidden for the same reason as 9/6.

window_lite_pattern.rule: Small rectangular lights in a leaded or muntined casement, not the Georgian sash ladder.

variants.note: Set in a monumental round- or basket-arched stone surround; the door itself is plain and the surround carries the elaboration.
The inherited value is a Georgian catalog door and reads as domestic rather than as the entrance to a fortified-derived stone house.

entry_door.rule: A plain, heavy plank or panelled door within an elaborated round- or basket-arched stone surround — the surround, not the leaf, carries the style's statement.

variants.note: The style's own bound proportion pack (vignola-composite) names this order directly: its fused Ionic-volute-over-Corinthian-acanthus capital is 'a defensible formal echo of a style built at the exact historical seam between Gothic structure and Renaissance ornament.'
The style presumes a published Renaissance canon quoted from measured chateau drawings, not an abstracted vernacular reading.

order.rule: Bound only, and narrowly, at the round-arched or basket-arched stone door and window surrounds the style's own defining_characteristics name. It never governs the roof, the dormers, the turrets, the chimneys or the skyline, which are Gothic vocabulary this order does not touch.
order.note: Overrides an incorrect cascade: the family lineage walk lands on french-vernacular (via the norman-vernacular reference edge) and forbids the entire classical-apparatus group with the rule 'all three are vernacular/folk building traditions' — true of the farm buildings french-vernacular actually describes, and wrong for this style, which is emphatically not one. Restored per the style's own bound proportion pack and diagnostic_tells.

variants.note: Applied to the jamb of a door or window surround only; never free-standing.

A portico is a Beaux-Arts and Colonial move. Chateauesque is entered through a stone surround set flush in a load-bearing wall, not approached through a colonnade — see distinguished_from beaux-arts-american.

column.rule: Where the order appears at all it is engaged, never free-standing.

extent.value: door and window surrounds only; there is no continuous classical entablature run at the eaves

entablature.rule: No running eaves entablature. The style's own proportional_system states plainly that 'there is no governing module; proportion is set by the roof' — the roof and its dormers do the compositional work a continuous entablature does in Beaux-Arts or Colonial Revival.

applies_when.note: over a door or window surround only
over a door or window surround only

variants.note: A Beaux-Arts/Adam device.

pediment.rule: A small pediment may cap a door or window surround; it is not a roofline element. The dormer's own gable termination — which the style's defining_characteristics separately describe as terminating 'in pediments, finials, or crockets' — is roof furniture, not this classical-apparatus slot, and is carried on the dormer instead.

variants.note: A Beaux-Arts and Neoclassical Revival device across a flat wall; Chateauesque's wall is broken by towers and dormers, not by a pilastered rhythm.

pilaster.rule: Confined to the jambs of an opening surround, matching column.

modillion_dentil.rule: No continuous modillion or dentil course. The roof, not a classical cornice, terminates the wall.
modillion_dentil.note: Replaces an incorrect ancestor note (french-vernacular's 'no order-derived vocabulary at all', true of farm buildings and not of this style). The real reason is different: the style has no continuous classical cornice for a modillion or dentil course to run along in the first place — the eave is subordinate to, and frequently interrupted by, the roof and its wall dormers, per the style's own 'no governing module; proportion is set by the roof.'

balustrade.rule: No balustraded parapet or roofline balustrade of any kind; the roof itself is the termination.
balustrade.note: Replaces an incorrect ancestor note. The real reason is the style's own distinguished_from entry against beaux-arts-american, stated directly: 'Beaux-Arts is horizontal...and terminates in a balustrade or attic rather than a roof. Chateauesque is vertical...and defined by an enormous roof.' A balustraded parapet is precisely the device that would make a Chateauesque house read as Beaux-Arts.

variants.note: At the order, where bound — capitals only.
Beaux-Arts and Neoclassical Revival register.
Adam/Federal register.
Greek Doric register; unrelated to a French Renaissance-Gothic seam.

ornament_vocabulary.rule: This slot covers only the classical half of the style's genuinely bifurcated ornament. The dominant, primary ornament vocabulary — crockets, finials, tracery, late Gothic in register — is outside what this classical-apparatus slot can name; no slot in the current ontology holds a distinct late-Gothic ornament set, so it stays recorded in prose here rather than invented as a fake classical entry.

variants.note: The inherited value is drawn from a Chesapeake/Tidewater plantation programme with no bearing on a Gilded Age Newport or Hudson Valley estate; corrected here.
Same inherited plantation-programme error; this style's period and clientele have no such building.

outbuilding_types.rule: Estate outbuildings appropriate to an 1880-1910 Northeastern fortune — a gate lodge, a carriage house, stabling — composed at reduced scale in the same stone vocabulary as the main house, not a Southern plantation service yard.

variants.note: The inherited canonical value belongs to a Georgian domestic dooryard and understates the scale of an estate whose exemplars include Biltmore and Ochre Court.

fence_wall.rule: Stone wall or wrought-iron fence on stone piers, matching the house's own ashlar.
